option_description: Controls whether the HTTP/S channel uses TLS to encrypt all data in transit between client and application. When false, all PII transmitted over the channel is exposed in plaintext to any observer on the network path.
security_impact: Directly gates the plaintext_transmission and absent_mutual_tls_authentication rules. The Rego policy fires plaintext_transmission immediately if transport_encryption_enabled is false, and absent_mutual_tls_authentication triggers unconditionally when this is false because mTLS is impossible without a TLS session. This is the highest-priority flag in the policy: a single false value activates two separate exposure rules.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Probe the target endpoint to confirm whether TLS is negotiated. A successful handshake confirms encryption is active.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should show a TLS protocol version and cipher suite. 'Verify return code: 0 (ok)' confirms a valid TLS session is established.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the web server TLS listener configuration to verify ssl/tls is enabled on the listening socket.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of ssl_certificate and ssl_certificate_key directives (nginx) or SSLEngine on with SSLCertificateFile (Apache) confirms TLS is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a plain HTTP connection to the service port to determine if it responds without TLS negotiation, which would indicate encryption is absent.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If TLS is enforced, either the plain HTTP connection is refused, times out, or receives a redirect (301/308) to HTTPS. If an HTTP 200 is returned over port 80 with PII-bearing paths accessible, transport_encryption_enabled should be set to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In AWS Console, navigate to EC2 > Load Balancers > select the ALB/NLB > Listeners tab. Confirm all listeners use HTTPS (port 443) with a TLS certificate assigned. In GCP Console, check Load Balancing > select frontend configuration for HTTPS protocol.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > EC2 > Load Balancers > [target LB] > Listeners tab | GCP Console > Network Services > Load Balancing > Frontend Configuration
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All PII-bearing listeners show Protocol: HTTPS with a valid SSL/TLS certificate ARN or resource ID attached.

typical_values: true (HTTPS-only deployment with TLS termination at load balancer or application server)
false (legacy HTTP-only service, internal microservice on plain TCP, or misconfigured listener)

option_description: Identifies the specific application-layer protocol used to carry PII data between the client and server. This determines the baseline security posture of the channel before any additional controls are applied.
security_impact: Referenced directly in the plaintext_transmission Rego rule. If protocol_scheme is any of http, ftp, smtp, ws, telnet, tcp_plain, or other_plain AND tls_redirect_enforced is false, the plaintext_transmission exposure fires. The value provides specificity beyond the boolean transport_encryption_enabled flag, enabling precise identification of which insecure protocol is in use.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture the initial handshake bytes from the service to identify the protocol in use. TLS-secured protocols begin with a TLS ClientHello; plaintext protocols show application-layer headers immediately.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: nmap identifies the service type (http, https, ftp, smtp, etc.) and whether SSL/TLS wrapping is detected per port.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect application and reverse proxy configuration files for the protocol scheme used in upstream, listener, and connection string definitions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: URL prefixes and listen directives reveal the protocol scheme. Look for http:// vs https://, ws:// vs wss://, etc.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the AWS API Gateway or Azure API Management configuration to retrieve the protocol scheme for each API endpoint definition.
how_to_obtain.command: aws apigateway get-rest-apis --query 'items[*].[name,id]' --output table && aws apigateway get-stages --rest-api-id <api-id> --query 'item[*].{Stage:stageName,HTTPS:defaultRouteSettings}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: API Gateway endpoints are always HTTPS; result confirms scheme. For on-premises APIs, substitute with the appropriate CLI or management API query.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review access logs to identify the scheme used in actual client requests. Log entries typically record the scheme or the server port, which implies the protocol.
how_to_obtain.command: awk '{print $7}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | grep -oP '^https?|^ftp|^ws' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Frequency counts of protocol schemes appearing in request URIs. Any count of http:// requests indicates plaintext traffic is reaching the server.

typical_values: https (standard web application and API traffic with TLS)
http (legacy or internal service without TLS, development environments)
wss (WebSocket over TLS for real-time applications)
ws (unencrypted WebSocket, common in misconfigured internal chat or notification services)
tcp_tls (custom TLS-wrapped TCP service such as a proprietary data feed)

option_description: Controls whether the server or load balancer automatically redirects any plaintext HTTP request to HTTPS, combined with HSTS headers to prevent future plaintext attempts. Ensures that even clients initiating unencrypted connections are upgraded before any PII is transmitted.
security_impact: Used as a compensating control in the plaintext_transmission Rego rule. When protocol_scheme is a plaintext value (http, ftp, ws, etc.), the rule fires only if tls_redirect_enforced is also false. Setting this to true prevents the plaintext_transmission exposure from triggering for services that accept HTTP on port 80 but immediately redirect to HTTPS, provided no PII is present in the initial redirect request.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send a plain HTTP request to port 80 and observe whether a 301 or 308 redirect to HTTPS is returned before any application content is served.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response should be HTTP/1.1 301 or 308 with a Location header pointing to https://<host>/. Any 200 OK on plain HTTP means the redirect is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check web server or load balancer configuration for HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect rules and HSTS header injection.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of 'return 301 https://$host$request_uri' in nginx or 'Redirect permanent / https://<host>/' in Apache, plus a Strict-Transport-Security header directive.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In AWS Console for ALB, check the HTTP:80 listener rule action. It should be 'Redirect to HTTPS' with status code 301 or 308. In Cloudflare, navigate to SSL/TLS > Edge Certificates and verify 'Always Use HTTPS' is enabled.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > EC2 > Load Balancers > [ALB] > Listeners > HTTP:80 > View/edit rules | Cloudflare Dashboard > SSL/TLS > Edge Certificates > Always Use HTTPS toggle
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The HTTP:80 listener action shows 'Redirect to https://#{host}:443/#{path}?#{query}' with status code 301 or 308. Cloudflare toggle is ON.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check HTTP response headers for the Strict-Transport-Security header, which is required alongside the redirect to prevent future plain HTTP connections.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload — presence confirms HSTS is configured alongside the redirect.

typical_values: true (ALB with HTTP:80 redirect rule, nginx return 301 https, HSTS header present)
false (HTTP-only service with no redirect, API server listening only on port 80, legacy application serving both HTTP and HTTPS)

option_description: Specifies the lowest TLS/SSL protocol version the server will accept during handshake negotiation. Versions below TLS 1.2 contain known cryptographic vulnerabilities that allow attackers to decrypt or manipulate session traffic.
security_impact: Central to two Rego rules. The tls_downgrade_attack rule fires if minimum_tls_version is SSLv2, SSLv3, TLSv1.0, or TLSv1.1. The weak_cipher_suite_negotiation rule also fires independently for the same set of weak versions because old protocol versions mandate or permit weak cipher suites. Accepting TLS 1.0 or 1.1 exposes the channel to POODLE, BEAST, DROWN, and related downgrade attacks even if the preferred version is TLS 1.3.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use testssl.sh to perform a comprehensive TLS protocol scan and identify the lowest accepted protocol version.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each protocol line shows 'offered' or 'not offered'. Only TLSv1.2 and TLSv1.3 should show 'offered'. Any older version showing 'offered' means the minimum is set too low.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect TLS protocol directives in the web server or load balancer configuration to identify the minimum accepted version.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: nginx: 'ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;' — Apache: 'SSLProtocol -All +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3' — HAProxy: 'ssl-min-ver TLSv1.2'. Absence of older protocol names is the secure state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to force a TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 handshake to confirm whether the server rejects these versions.
how_to_obtain.command: openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -tls1 2>&1 | grep -E 'handshake|alert|DONE|Protocol' ; openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -tls1_1 2>&1 | grep -E 'handshake|alert|DONE|Protocol'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'handshake failure' or 'alert protocol version' confirms TLS 1.0/1.1 are rejected. 'CONNECTED' followed by a protocol line indicates these weak versions are accepted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In AWS Console, check the security policy on your ALB or CloudFront distribution. For CloudFront, navigate to Distributions > [distribution] > Security Policy dropdown. For ALB, check the HTTPS listener's security policy.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > CloudFront > Distributions > [dist] > General > Security Policy | EC2 > Load Balancers > [ALB] > Listeners > HTTPS:443 > Security Policy
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure policies include ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 or ELBSecurityPolicy-FS-1-2-Res-2020-10. Policies containing 'TLS-1-0' or 'TLS-1-1' indicate the minimum is too low.

typical_values: TLSv1.2 (most common secure baseline for production web services)
TLSv1.0 (legacy applications supporting old clients, considered weak)
TLSv1.1 (transitional configuration, still present in older load balancer default policies)

option_description: Indicates whether an active mechanism prevents TLS protocol downgrade attacks. This includes TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV (RFC 7507), which signals to the server that the client is capable of higher protocol versions, and HSTS preloading, which prevents clients from attempting plain HTTP connections.
security_impact: Directly referenced in the tls_downgrade_attack Rego rule: if downgrade_protection_enabled is false, the rule fires unconditionally regardless of the minimum_tls_version setting. This means even a server configured for TLS 1.2+ minimum can be flagged if TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV is not advertised, because an active attacker can interfere with the ClientHello to force an incomplete handshake and retry at a lower version.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use testssl.sh to verify TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV support, which is the primary server-side downgrade protection mechanism.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV (RFC 7507): Supported' confirms downgrade protection is active. 'Not supported' means downgrade_protection_enabled should be set to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for HSTS preload header in the HTTPS response, which is a client-side downgrade prevention mechanism complementary to TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sI https://<host>/ | grep -i 'strict-transport-security' && curl -sI https://<host>/ | grep -i 'preload'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Strict-Transport-Security header with 'preload' directive and max-age >= 31536000 confirms HSTS-based downgrade protection is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Java SSL configuration for jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms which controls fallback prevention, or OpenSSL configuration for explicit TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV support.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: java.security should list SSLv3, TLSv1, TLSv1.1 in jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms. OpenSSL builds after 1.0.1j include TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV by default.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Manually attempt a downgrade by sending a ClientHello with TLS 1.0 and the FALLBACK_SCSV pseudo-cipher to verify the server rejects it with an inappropriate_fallback alert.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'alert inappropriate fallback' confirms the server correctly rejects the downgrade attempt. No alert or successful connection means downgrade protection is absent.

typical_values: true (modern OpenSSL/BoringSSL with TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV enabled, HSTS with preload, AWS ALB with modern security policy)
false (legacy Java applications using old JSSE, older nginx builds, custom TCP proxies without SCSV support)

option_description: An explicit list of deprecated protocol versions (SSLv2, SSLv3, TLSv1.0, TLSv1.1) that are actively enabled in server or client TLS configuration. Each entry in this list represents a specific known-vulnerable protocol version that increases the attack surface for downgrade exploitation.
security_impact: The tls_downgrade_attack Rego rule fires if count(deprecated_ssl_protocols_enabled) is greater than zero. Any non-empty array triggers the exposure, regardless of what the minimum_tls_version is set to. This attribute captures explicit opt-in to weak protocols via configuration directives such as adding SSLv3 back to a previously hardened configuration, which is a separate signal from the minimum version setting.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run testssl.sh against the endpoint to enumerate all accepted protocol versions and extract any deprecated ones.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any line showing 'offered' for SSLv2, SSLv3, TLSv1, or TLSv1.1 means that protocol should be added to the deprecated_ssl_protocols_enabled array. Empty output is the secure state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search all TLS configuration files for protocol directives that explicitly include deprecated versions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any match indicates a deprecated protocol is explicitly configured. Example: 'ssl_protocols TLSv1 TLSv1.1 TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3' means TLSv1.0 and TLSv1.1 are in the deprecated list.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers script to retrieve the full list of accepted protocols per port.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each accepted protocol version is listed with its supported ciphers. SSLv3, TLSv1.0, or TLSv1.1 sections appearing in output should populate this array.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the cloud provider API for the TLS security policy applied to load balancers, then cross-reference policy names against the known cipher/protocol inclusions.
how_to_obtain.command: aws elbv2 describe-ssl-policies --names $(aws elbv2 describe-listeners --load-balancer-arn <lb-arn> --query 'Listeners[?Protocol==`HTTPS`].SslPolicy' --output text) --query 'SslPolicies[*].{Name:Name,Protocols:SslProtocols}' --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output shows the SslProtocols array for the applied policy. Any appearance of TLSv1 or TLSv1.1 means those should be in deprecated_ssl_protocols_enabled.

typical_values: [] (empty — secure state, no deprecated protocols enabled)
["TLSv1.0", "TLSv1.1"] (common legacy state on older ALB default policies or unconverted nginx configs)
["SSLv3"] (severely misconfigured or very old server, vulnerable to POODLE)
["TLSv1.1"] (transitional state during migration away from TLS 1.1)

option_description: The explicit list of TLS cipher suite identifiers (in IANA or OpenSSL naming format) that are permitted during TLS negotiation on the server or load balancer. This list defines the complete set of algorithms available for key exchange, authentication, encryption, and MAC during each TLS session.
security_impact: The weak_cipher_suite_negotiation Rego rule applies a regex match against this array looking for cipher names containing RC4, NULL, EXP, EXPORT, ADH, AECDH, aNULL, DES (non-3DES), eNULL, IDEA, SEED, RC2, or ANON. Any match triggers the exposure. This attribute must be populated accurately for the rule to function — an empty or null array bypasses regex detection and relies on the cipher_suite_policy_enforced flag to catch weak cipher risks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use testssl.sh to enumerate all cipher suites accepted by the server and extract their OpenSSL names.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table of accepted ciphers grouped by protocol. The full list of cipher suite names should be captured and used to populate allowed_cipher_suites.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract the cipher suite string directly from the TLS configuration directives in the web server or proxy configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A cipher string such as 'ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:...' — expand this with 'openssl ciphers -v <cipher_string>' to get individual cipher names.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Expand an OpenSSL cipher string into its constituent cipher suite identifiers for accurate documentation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A sorted list of individual cipher suite names (e.g., ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256) that are actually enabled. This list populates allowed_cipher_suites.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nmap to perform live cipher suite enumeration against the target, producing a list of all server-accepted ciphers without relying on config file access.
how_to_obtain.command: nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 <host> 2>/dev/null | grep '|' | grep -v 'NULL\|compressors\|cipher preference\|least strength' | awk '{print $2}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Indented cipher suite names under each protocol section. The full enumerated list should be used to populate allowed_cipher_suites.

typical_values: ["ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256", "ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384", "AES128-GCM-SHA256", "RC4-SHA"] (mixed — contains weak RC4, would trigger the rule)
["ALL:!aNULL:!eNULL"] (unexpanded OpenSSL string, must be resolved to individual suites for accurate assessment)

option_description: Indicates whether the server uses an explicit allowlist-based cipher suite policy — meaning only specifically approved cipher suites are permitted — rather than accepting whatever the TLS library or platform offers by default. An allowlist approach prevents weak ciphers from being silently enabled by library upgrades or default configurations.
security_impact: The weak_cipher_suite_negotiation Rego rule fires if cipher_suite_policy_enforced is false, independently of what allowed_cipher_suites contains. This means that even if no explicitly weak ciphers are listed, the absence of a deliberate allowlist policy is itself flagged as an exposure because library defaults may silently include weak options that have not been reviewed. This attribute enforces the principle that security configurations must be explicit, not inherited.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether an explicit cipher suite directive is present and uses an allowlist form (specific named ciphers) rather than a denylist (using ! negations against defaults) or is absent entirely.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count greater than 0 per file indicates a cipher directive exists. Then inspect the value: a curated list of specific cipher names (not 'DEFAULT' or library placeholders) indicates an allowlist policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run testssl.sh and check whether the server accepts any ciphers outside of a known-good set, which would indicate the policy is not strictly enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output of 0 means no weak ciphers are accepted, consistent with an enforced allowlist. Any non-zero count means weak ciphers are present and cipher_suite_policy_enforced should be false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the infrastructure or platform team to determine whether cipher suite configuration is managed via an approved baseline (e.g., CIS Benchmark, Mozilla TLS configuration), or is left to framework/library defaults with no explicit override.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented cipher policy referencing a specific standard (Mozilla 'Intermediate' or 'Modern' profile, NIST SP 800-52r2, AWS ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2) with evidence of enforcement in configuration management (Ansible, Terraform, Chef) confirms the policy is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud-managed TLS termination, verify that a named security policy (not the default) has been explicitly set on all HTTPS listeners, confirming deliberate cipher policy selection.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each HTTPS listener should show a specific named policy (e.g., ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06) rather than the default 'ELBSecurityPolicy-2016-08'. Explicit named policy selection constitutes an enforced allowlist.

typical_values: true (nginx with explicit ssl_ciphers directive using Mozilla Modern profile, Apache with SSLCipherSuite specifying ECDHE+AESGCM:ECDHE+AES, HAProxy with explicit ssl-default-bind-ciphers)

false (web server installed with default TLS configuration and no ssl_ciphers override, Spring Boot with default SSLContext and no cipher suite property set, Node.js https.createServer without ciphers option)

option_description: Controls whether the HTTP client enforces full X.509 certificate chain validation against trusted CA roots when establishing TLS connections. When enabled, the client verifies every certificate in the server's presented chain up to a trusted root CA anchor, rejecting connections where the chain is incomplete, self-signed, or untrusted.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'Missing Certificate Validation' exposure (score 8, criticality high) whenever `not input.certificate_chain_validation_enabled` evaluates to true. Disabling chain validation means the client will accept any certificate presented by a server, including those generated on-the-fly by a man-in-the-middle proxy. This directly enables MITRE T1553.004 (Install Root Certificate) and T1587.003 (Digital Certificates) attacks, allowing adversaries to intercept and decrypt PII in transit without client detection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search application source code for Python requests library calls that suppress certificate verification using the verify=False flag.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No matches indicates chain validation is not suppressed. Any match with verify=False means certificate_chain_validation_enabled should be set to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan Go source files for InsecureSkipVerify=true in TLS configuration structs, which disables certificate chain validation in Go HTTP clients.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No matches indicates chain validation is active. Any match means certificate_chain_validation_enabled should be set to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search Node.js source files for rejectUnauthorized:false or NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 settings that disable certificate validation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No matches indicates validation is enforced. Matches with false or 0 indicate certificate_chain_validation_enabled should be set to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan Java source for custom TrustManager implementations that override checkServerTrusted with empty bodies, which accept all certificates regardless of chain.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Legitimate implementations delegate to the default trust manager. An empty or catch-all checkServerTrusted body means certificate_chain_validation_enabled should be set to false.

option_description: Controls whether the HTTP client verifies that the Common Name (CN) or Subject Alternative Names (SANs) in the server's TLS certificate match the hostname being connected to. This check prevents a valid certificate issued for one domain from being used to impersonate a different domain.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'Missing Certificate Validation' exposure (score 8, criticality high) when `not input.hostname_verification_enabled` is true. Without hostname verification, an attacker possessing any CA-signed certificate—regardless of which domain it was issued for—can perform a man-in-the-middle attack. Even with chain validation enabled, the connection is vulnerable if the hostname is not checked. This exposure maps to MITRE T1553.004 and T1587.003, enabling fraudulent certificate use against PII-bearing channels.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search Java source code for use of ALLOW_ALL_HOSTNAME_VERIFIER or NoopHostnameVerifier, which disable hostname matching in Apache HttpClient and similar libraries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Use of ALLOW_ALL_HOSTNAME_VERIFIER or NoopHostnameVerifier indicates hostname_verification_enabled should be set to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Python source for ssl.match_hostname being disabled or ssl.CERT_NONE being passed to ssl context, which bypasses hostname verification.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of check_hostname=False or CERT_NONE indicates hostname_verification_enabled should be set to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use curl to attempt a TLS connection presenting a certificate with a mismatched hostname. If the connection succeeds, hostname verification is not enforced by the server-side expectation or the client being tested.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A properly configured client should produce 'SSL: certificate subject name does not match target host name' or equivalent. A successful connection indicates hostname_verification_enabled is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search Node.js code and environment for checkServerIdentity overrides or global TLS option disabling hostname checks.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A checkServerIdentity that returns undefined without performing checks indicates hostname_verification_enabled should be set to false.

option_description: Specifies the mechanism the HTTP client uses to check whether server certificates have been revoked before the CA's stated expiry. Valid modes are: 'ocsp' (real-time Online Certificate Status Protocol query), 'crl' (Certificate Revocation List download and check), 'ocsp_stapling' (server-provided OCSP response stapled to the TLS handshake), or 'none' (no revocation checking performed).
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'Missing Certificate Validation' exposure when `input.certificate_chain_validation_enabled == true` AND `input.certificate_revocation_check_mode == 'none'`. This means even a correctly validated chain is insufficient if revocation is not checked: a certificate that has been compromised and revoked by the CA will still be accepted by the client, allowing an attacker who has obtained a stolen or mis-issued certificate to perform man-in-the-middle attacks on PII. This maps to MITRE T1553.004 (Install Root Certificate) and T1587.003 (Digital Certificates).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Java application TLS configuration or JVM startup properties for OCSP and CRL flags passed to the JVM security provider.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of com.sun.security.enableCRLDP=true indicates CRL mode. ocsp.enable=true indicates OCSP mode. No such flags means none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Python applications, check if pyOpenSSL or ssl context is configured with revocation callbacks or OCSP settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of OCSP callback registration indicates ocsp mode. Absence of any revocation configuration means the value is none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use OpenSSL to perform a TLS handshake with OCSP stapling enabled and check whether the server returns a stapled OCSP response.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If 'OCSP Response Status: successful' appears, the server supports ocsp_stapling. If absent, the client must actively query OCSP or use CRL, or revocation checking is none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview application developers or review API gateway/service mesh documentation to determine if revocation checking is explicitly configured at the framework or infrastructure level.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation confirming CRL endpoints, OCSP responder URLs, or stapling configuration maps to the respective mode. No documented configuration maps to none.

option_description: Indicates whether the HTTP client is configured to accept TLS certificates that are self-signed (not issued by a recognized CA), either through explicit trust store additions, custom TrustManager logic, or verification bypass flags. When true, the client will establish TLS connections to servers presenting self-signed certificates without a valid chain of trust.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'Missing Certificate Validation' exposure (score 8, criticality high) whenever `input.self_signed_certificates_accepted == true`. Accepting self-signed certificates is functionally equivalent to disabling certificate validation, because any attacker can generate a self-signed certificate for any domain and present it during interception. This enables trivial man-in-the-middle attacks against PII-bearing HTTPS flows, corresponding to MITRE T1553.004 and T1587.003. This setting is frequently introduced during development and left enabled in production.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search application trust store configuration and source code for custom trust store files or inline self-signed certificate imports that would cause them to be trusted.
how_to_obtain.command: find /path/to/app/ -name '*.jks' -o -name '*.p12' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name 'truststore*' 2>/dev/null | xargs -I{} keytool -list -keystore {} -storepass changeit 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'self\|Entry type: trustedCertEntry'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A custom trust store containing entries not rooted to a public CA indicates self-signed certificates may be accepted. Review each entry's issuer equals subject (self-signed indicator).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Grep source code for patterns where SSL context is populated with self-signed certificate files or where certificate verification is bypassed specifically to allow self-signed certs.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any match indicates self_signed_certificates_accepted should be set to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use openssl to generate a temporary self-signed certificate and attempt a connection to the target using a test proxy. Alternatively, test the client against a server presenting a self-signed cert and observe whether the connection is rejected.
how_to_obtain.command: openssl s_client -connect <target_host>:443 -verify_return_error 2>&1 | grep -E 'verify error|self signed|Verify return code'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If the client application accepts a connection when 'verify error:num=18:self signed certificate' is present in the server's cert chain, self_signed_certificates_accepted is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect environment variable configuration and CI/CD pipeline settings for NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED or similar variables that may implicitly enable self-signed certificate acceptance at runtime.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 or an empty/non-existent REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE pointing to a bundle containing self-signed certs indicates self_signed_certificates_accepted is true.

option_description: Controls whether the server requires the connecting client to present a valid X.509 client certificate during the TLS handshake (mutual TLS / mTLS). When true, both server and client are cryptographically authenticated before any application data is exchanged, binding the connection to a verified client identity.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'Absent Mutual TLS Authentication' exposure (criticality medium, score 5) when `input.transport_encryption_enabled == true` AND `not input.mutual_tls_required`. Without mTLS, any client that can reach the network endpoint can inject requests into the PII data flow. The server cannot cryptographically bind transmitted PII to a verified client identity, enabling unauthorized data injection and impersonation. This maps to MITRE T1588.004 (Digital Certificates) and T1649 (Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates). Note the policy also fires when transport encryption is absent entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect nginx TLS configuration for ssl_verify_client directive, which controls whether client certificates are required, optional, or disabled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ssl_verify_client on; indicates mutual_tls_required is true. ssl_verify_client off; or absence of the directive indicates false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Apache HTTP Server configuration for SSLVerifyClient directive that mandates client certificate presentation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SSLVerifyClient require indicates mutual_tls_required is true. SSLVerifyClient none or absence indicates false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a TLS connection to the target without presenting a client certificate. If the server rejects the handshake, mTLS is enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A response containing 'alert certificate required' or TLS handshake failure without a client cert indicates mutual_tls_required is true. A successful connection without client cert means false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query API gateway or service mesh (e.g., Istio, Kong, AWS API Gateway) management API to retrieve mTLS policy settings for the relevant service or route.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Mode STRICT indicates mutual_tls_required is true. Mode PERMISSIVE or DISABLE indicates false. For Kong, check TLS client certificate plugin configuration.

option_description: Specifies the application-layer mechanism used to prevent replay attacks on PII-bearing HTTP/S requests. Valid values are: 'nonce' (a unique random value included in each request and validated server-side for single use), 'sequence_number' (a monotonically increasing counter tied to a session, rejected if out of order), 'timestamp_with_strict_window' (request includes a timestamp; server rejects requests outside a narrow time window, typically ±30 seconds), or 'none' (no replay protection present).
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Replay Attack on PII Requests' (criticality medium, score 5) when `input.replay_protection_mechanism == 'none'`. It also fires when a mechanism is declared but `not input.server_side_replay_validation_enforced` and `not input.request_idempotency_key_required`, meaning declaring a mechanism without enforcing it is treated as no protection. Without replay protection, a captured valid PII-bearing request can be retransmitted by an attacker to trigger repeated processing, unauthorized state changes, or data enumeration, corresponding to MITRE T1565.002 (Transmitted Data Manipulation) and T1020.001 (Traffic Duplication).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review API design documentation, OpenAPI/Swagger specifications, and request schema definitions for nonce, X-Request-ID, sequence, or timestamp fields that are mandatory in request headers or bodies.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Mandatory nonce or sequence fields in request schema indicate the corresponding mechanism. Absence of any such field indicates none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review application request logs to determine whether nonce, sequence, or timestamp fields are present and populated in incoming PII-bearing requests.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Repeated nonce or timestamp fields in log entries confirm the mechanism is in use. Their absence in requests involving PII endpoints indicates none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture a valid authenticated PII-bearing request using a proxy tool and replay it immediately. Observe whether the server accepts or rejects the duplicate request.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTTP 409 Conflict, HTTP 400 Bad Request with a replay/duplicate error, or a nonce-already-used error message indicates protection is active. HTTP 200 on replay indicates none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search middleware and authentication filter code for nonce validation logic, sequence counter checks, or timestamp window enforcement.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Server-side nonce store lookups, sequence increment checks, or timestamp comparison logic confirms the mechanism type. Absence indicates none.

option_description: Indicates whether the server actively validates replay protection tokens—nonces, sequence numbers, or timestamps—included in incoming requests, and enforces rejection of duplicate or out-of-window requests. This is distinct from merely accepting these values in requests; the server must actively maintain state to validate uniqueness or ordering and return an error on violations.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'Replay Attack on PII Requests' (criticality medium, score 5) when `input.replay_protection_mechanism != 'none'` but BOTH `not input.server_side_replay_validation_enforced` AND `not input.request_idempotency_key_required`. This reflects that declaring a replay protection mechanism without enforcing it server-side provides no actual protection. An attacker who captures a valid PII request can replay it repeatedly if the server never checks whether the nonce was already used or the timestamp is stale. This corresponds to MITRE T1565.002 and T1020.001.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search server-side request handling code for nonce store lookups, Redis/memcached SETNX operations, or database uniqueness checks on nonce values that confirm server-side validation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of nonce existence checks against a persistent or in-memory store confirms server_side_replay_validation_enforced is true. Absence means false even if nonces are accepted in requests.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a controlled replay test: capture a valid PII-bearing request with a nonce or timestamp, wait beyond any expected processing time, and replay the identical request. Confirm the server rejects it.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -v -X POST https://<target_host>/api/pii-endpoint -H 'X-Nonce: <captured_nonce>' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -d '<payload>' && sleep 2 && curl -v -X POST https://<target_host>/api/pii-endpoint -H 'X-Nonce: <same_captured_nonce>' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -d '<payload>'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Second request returning HTTP 409/400 with 'nonce already used' or 'duplicate request' error indicates server_side_replay_validation_enforced is true. Second request returning HTTP 200 means false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review application and security logs for replay rejection events, duplicate nonce detection log entries, or timestamp window violation messages.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing replay rejection events indicate server_side_replay_validation_enforced is true. No such events (even when replays occur) indicates false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview application developers and review server-side middleware or filter chain documentation to confirm that nonce/timestamp validation middleware is registered and active in the request processing pipeline for PII endpoints.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation that a replay validation filter is registered before PII endpoint handlers, with a backing store for seen nonces or timestamp comparison logic, indicates true. Absence of such middleware indicates false.

option_description: Indicates whether the API requires clients to supply an idempotency key (typically a client-generated UUID in a header such as Idempotency-Key) that the server validates and stores to prevent duplicate processing of the same PII-bearing request. The server must persist seen keys with an appropriate TTL and return a consistent cached response rather than reprocessing when a duplicate key is received.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses this attribute as a secondary guard against replay attacks: 'Replay Attack on PII Requests' fires when `input.replay_protection_mechanism != 'none'` AND `not input.server_side_replay_validation_enforced` AND `not input.request_idempotency_key_required`. Idempotency keys serve dual purpose—they prevent duplicate processing from both accidental client retries and malicious replay attacks. Without idempotency key enforcement, a captured PII-bearing request can be replayed to trigger multiple state changes (e.g., repeated data submissions or financial transactions), corresponding to MITRE T1565.002 (Transmitted Data Manipulation) and T1020.001 (Traffic Duplication).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect API gateway configuration (e.g., Kong, AWS API Gateway, Apigee) for idempotency key plugin or policy enforcement settings on PII-handling routes.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An idempotency plugin configured and enabled on PII routes with validation=true and a TTL indicates request_idempotency_key_required is true. Absence or optional enforcement means false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send a PII-bearing POST request without an Idempotency-Key header to a target endpoint. If the server processes the request without complaint, the key is not required.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -v -X POST https://<target_host>/api/pii-endpoint -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"pii":"test"}' 2>&1 | grep -E 'HTTP/|Idempotency|400|422|required'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTTP 400 or 422 with a body mentioning missing Idempotency-Key indicates request_idempotency_key_required is true. HTTP 200/201 without the header means false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search server-side code for idempotency key header extraction, storage, and lookup logic that would enforce uniqueness of request processing.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Code that extracts the Idempotency-Key header, checks it against a persistent store, and returns a cached response on duplicate indicates request_idempotency_key_required is true. Absence of such logic means false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the API's OpenAPI or AsyncAPI specification for the Idempotency-Key header marked as required on PII-handling POST, PUT, or PATCH operations.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s https://<target_host>/openapi.json | python3 -c "import sys,json; spec=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(p,m,spec['paths'][p][m].get('parameters','')) for p in spec.get('paths',{}) for m in spec['paths'][p]]" 2>/dev/null | grep -i idempotency
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Idempotency-Key parameter marked as 'required: true' on relevant operations indicates request_idempotency_key_required is true. Optional or absent header definition means false.

option_description: The application-layer mechanism used to ensure message integrity beyond transport-layer protections. Controls whether HMAC, digital signatures, JWT signatures, or no integrity mechanism is applied to payloads before transmission between clients and backend applications.
security_impact: Directly referenced by the message_integrity_not_enforced Rego rule. When this value is 'none', the policy triggers an exposure if TLS is terminated at an intermediary without re-encryption, or if TLS termination state is unknown. Without application-layer integrity, a malicious intermediary (e.g., a compromised load balancer) can modify PII payloads in transit without detection, matching MITRE T1565.002 (Transmitted Data Manipulation).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect API gateway configuration files for HMAC or JWT signature enforcement settings. For AWS API Gateway, review the stage or method request configuration for authorizer types. For Kong, check plugin configurations for request-signing or jwt plugins.
how_to_obtain.file_path: /etc/kong/kong.conf or kong.yml plugin definitions; AWS API Gateway stage export JSON
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of 'hmac-auth', 'jwt', or 'request-transformer' plugin entries with signing configuration, or absence thereof indicating 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect application middleware or source code for HMAC or signature generation before outbound requests. Search the codebase for relevant signing libraries or JWT creation calls.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Matching lines indicate an integrity mechanism is in use; no results indicate 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the message broker or API gateway management API to retrieve integration configuration. For AWS API Gateway, use the CLI to describe method responses and integration request parameters.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Review 'requestParameters' and 'requestTemplates' for presence of signature headers or HMAC fields.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect outbound request logs or message broker traces to determine if Authorization or X-Signature headers containing HMAC or JWT values are consistently present on PII-bearing requests.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Consistent presence of signing headers on requests indicates an active integrity mechanism; absence indicates 'none'.

option_description: Indicates whether TLS is terminated at an intermediary such as a load balancer, reverse proxy, or CDN before traffic reaches the backend application. When true, the backend receives decrypted traffic from the intermediary rather than encrypted client traffic.
security_impact: Referenced by the message_integrity_not_enforced Rego rule in conjunction with app_layer_integrity_mechanism and backend_transport_reencrypted. When TLS is terminated at an intermediary and no application-layer integrity mechanism exists, the policy flags a message integrity exposure. This is because the intermediary can read and potentially alter PII payloads in the cleartext segment between the termination point and the backend.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect load balancer or reverse proxy configuration files to determine if SSL/TLS termination is configured on the listener. Look for 'ssl_certificate' directives paired with upstream blocks that use plain HTTP.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NGINX: 'listen 443 ssl;' with upstream 'proxy_pass http://backend' (plain HTTP) confirms TLS termination at intermediary. HAProxy: 'bind *:443 ssl' with 'server backend 10.0.0.1:80' confirms termination.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the AWS Management Console and inspect the load balancer listener configuration. For ALB, check if the HTTPS listener forwards to target groups using HTTP or HTTPS protocol.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > EC2 > Load Balancers > [Select ALB] > Listeners tab > View/Edit Rules > Check target group protocol (HTTP = TLS terminated at ALB)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Target group protocol showing 'HTTP' on port 80 confirms TLS is terminated at the ALB. Target group showing 'HTTPS' on port 443 indicates re-encryption.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the AWS CLI to describe the target group configuration and determine the protocol used for backend communication.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Protocol column showing 'HTTP' confirms TLS termination at the load balancer intermediary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture traffic on the backend server's network interface to determine if it receives plaintext HTTP or encrypted TLS traffic from the load balancer.
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i eth0 -nn port 80 or port 8080 -A -c 20 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'HTTP|GET|POST|Host:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Readable HTTP request headers appearing in tcpdump output on the backend confirms TLS is terminated at an upstream intermediary.

option_description: Whether the connection from a TLS-terminating intermediary to the backend application is re-encrypted with TLS, ensuring end-to-end encryption even when an intermediary inspects traffic. When false, traffic between the intermediary and backend travels as plaintext over the internal network.
security_impact: Referenced by the message_integrity_not_enforced Rego rule. When TLS is terminated at an intermediary and backend_transport_reencrypted is false, and no application-layer integrity mechanism is present, the policy triggers a message integrity exposure. Plaintext internal traffic is vulnerable to lateral movement interception, rogue insider access, and manipulation by any process or service with access to the internal network segment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the reverse proxy or load balancer upstream configuration to determine if the backend connection uses HTTPS/TLS or plain HTTP. Check for SSL/TLS directives in the upstream block.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NGINX: 'proxy_pass https://backend' or 'proxy_ssl on' indicates re-encryption. HAProxy: 'server backend 10.0.0.1:443 ssl verify required' indicates re-encryption. Plain 'http://' or port 80 indicates no re-encryption.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the AWS CLI to check if the ALB target group uses HTTPS protocol for backend communication, confirming re-encryption is configured.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Protocol': 'HTTPS' and 'Port': 443 confirm backend re-encryption is enabled. 'Protocol': 'HTTP' confirms no re-encryption.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the backend server, capture traffic on the expected backend port and determine if it is TLS-encrypted or plaintext by attempting to read packet contents.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Unreadable binary/encrypted content on the capture confirms TLS re-encryption. Readable HTTP headers confirm plaintext internal traffic (no re-encryption).

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the AWS Console, inspect the target group protocol and verify TLS certificates are configured for backend health checks, which indicate HTTPS is used for the backend connection.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > EC2 > Target Groups > [Select Target Group] > Details tab > Protocol (must be HTTPS for re-encryption) and Health check settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Protocol: HTTPS and Health check protocol: HTTPS with a valid certificate configuration confirms backend re-encryption.

option_description: Whether the application sets the HTTP Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) response header on HTTPS responses. This header instructs browsers and HTTP clients to only connect to the application over HTTPS for the duration specified by max-age, preventing protocol downgrade before TLS is established.
security_impact: Directly referenced by the http_strict_transport_security_absent Rego rule. The policy triggers an exposure when this value is false, regardless of other HSTS settings. Without HSTS, clients may initiate plaintext HTTP connections on first visit or after cache expiry, which can be intercepted by an adversary positioned on the network before TLS upgrade occurs (MITRE T1562.010 Downgrade Attack, T1573 Encrypted Channel).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Make an HTTPS request to the application endpoint and inspect response headers for the presence of Strict-Transport-Security. Use curl with the -I flag to retrieve headers only.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains' or similar. No output indicates the header is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect web server configuration files for HSTS header directives. Check NGINX add_header, Apache Header directives, or application framework middleware configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of 'add_header Strict-Transport-Security' (NGINX) or 'Header always set Strict-Transport-Security' (Apache) confirms HSTS is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Open the application URL in a browser using developer tools. Navigate to the Network tab, select the initial HTTPS request, and inspect the Response Headers section for Strict-Transport-Security.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Browser DevTools (F12) > Network tab > Select first document request > Headers > Response Headers > look for 'strict-transport-security'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 'strict-transport-security' entry in response headers with a max-age value confirms HSTS is present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use a security scanning API or SSL Labs API to retrieve header analysis for the target domain, which reports HSTS presence as part of the SSL configuration assessment.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response containing 'hsts: true' or HSTS policy details confirms the header is present and correctly configured.

option_description: The numeric value of the max-age directive in the Strict-Transport-Security header, expressed in seconds. This value defines how long browsers must refuse to connect over plain HTTP after receiving the header. A value of 0 disables HSTS enforcement; NIST and OWASP recommend a minimum of 31536000 (1 year).
security_impact: Referenced by the http_strict_transport_security_absent Rego rule. The policy triggers an exposure when hsts_header_present is true but hsts_max_age_seconds is less than 31536000 (one year). A short max-age value shortens the window during which HSTS protects clients, allowing protocol downgrade attacks (T1562.010) after cache expiry, particularly for infrequent users or clients whose HSTS cache has been cleared.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the HTTPS response headers and extract the max-age value from the Strict-Transport-Security header using curl and awk or grep.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A numeric value such as '31536000' or '63072000'. No output or '0' indicates HSTS is absent or disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the web server or application framework configuration for the max-age value set in the HSTS header directive. Extract the numeric value from the configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Numeric value representing seconds; values below 31536000 are insufficient per OWASP and NIST guidance.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use browser developer tools to inspect the Strict-Transport-Security header value on the HTTPS response and read the max-age parameter.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Browser DevTools (F12) > Network tab > Select HTTPS document request > Response Headers > strict-transport-security > read max-age=<value>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: max-age value of 31536000 or greater satisfies OWASP minimum requirements. Values below this threshold trigger the exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Mozilla Observatory API to retrieve a structured analysis of security headers including the HSTS max-age value for the target domain.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output showing 'max-age' value and pass/fail status. A max-age below 31536000 shows as a failing result.

option_description: Whether the application accepts connections on unencrypted HTTP (typically port 80) without immediately redirecting clients to HTTPS. When true, PII requests may be initiated and partially transmitted over plaintext before any TLS upgrade can occur, creating an interception window even when HTTPS is also available.
security_impact: Referenced by the http_strict_transport_security_absent Rego rule. The policy triggers an exposure whenever http_plaintext_accessible is true, regardless of HSTS configuration. Plaintext HTTP access enables passive interception (T1040 Network Sniffing) and active man-in-the-middle attacks before TLS is established. Even with HSTS configured, new clients or clients with expired HSTS cache entries remain vulnerable on their initial HTTP connection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a direct HTTP connection to the application hostname on port 80 and observe the response code. A 200 response or non-redirect response confirms plaintext access is enabled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK' or '400 Bad Request' without a redirect confirms plaintext is accessible. 'HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently' with Location: https:// indicates redirect is in place (but verify HSTS is also set).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nmap to scan port 80 on the application host and determine if it is open and serving HTTP responses.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: '80/tcp open http' confirms the plaintext HTTP port is accessible. 'closed' or 'filtered' indicates port 80 is not accessible.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect load balancer or web server configuration to determine if port 80 listener is configured to redirect to HTTPS or serve content directly.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NGINX: 'return 301 https://$host$request_uri' under the port 80 server block confirms redirect. Absence of redirect or presence of 'proxy_pass' to backend confirms plaintext access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the application URL using plain HTTP in a browser and observe whether the browser is redirected to HTTPS or if content is served over HTTP.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Open browser > Navigate to http://<application-hostname>/ > Observe address bar: if it remains 'http://' and content loads, plaintext is accessible. If redirected to 'https://', verify the redirect response headers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Browser address bar staying on 'http://' with loaded content confirms plaintext accessibility. Automatic redirect to 'https://' indicates a redirect is in place.

option_description: Whether request rate limiting or bandwidth throttling controls are enforced on the PII data channel. This includes controls applied at the API gateway, application middleware, WAF rules, or service mesh level that restrict the number or volume of requests a client can make within a given time window.
security_impact: Referenced by the missing_rate_limiting_on_pii_channel Rego rule. The policy triggers an exposure when rate limiting is absent and either the channel requires no authentication or a bulk export endpoint is exposed. Without rate limiting, an adversary with channel access can automate high-volume PII extraction (MITRE T1020 Automated Exfiltration) or enumerate records at maximum throughput without triggering throttling controls (T1030 Data Transfer Size Limits).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Make repeated HTTP requests to the endpoint and inspect response headers for rate limit indicators. X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, or Retry-After headers confirm rate limiting is active.
how_to_obtain.command: for i in {1..10}; do curl -sI https://<application-hostname>/api/pii-endpoint -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' | grep -iE 'x-ratelimit|retry-after|429'; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of 'X-RateLimit-Limit', 'X-RateLimit-Remaining' headers or HTTP 429 Too Many Requests after threshold confirms rate limiting is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect API gateway configuration files (Kong, AWS API Gateway, NGINX) for rate limiting or throttle plugin or policy definitions applied to the relevant route or stage.
how_to_obtain.file_path: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf; /etc/kong/kong.yml; /app/config/api-gateway.yaml; AWS API Gateway stage throttling settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of 'limit_req_zone' (NGINX), 'rate-limiting' plugin (Kong), or throttling configuration in API gateway stage settings confirms rate limiting is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the AWS API Gateway console, navigate to the Usage Plans or Stage settings to verify if throttling (rate and burst limits) is configured for the API stage serving the PII endpoint.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > API Gateway > [Select API] > Stages > [Select Stage] > Default Route Throttling OR Usage Plans > [Select Plan] > Throttling settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-zero values for 'Rate (requests per second)' and 'Burst' confirm rate limiting is enabled. Zero or absent values confirm rate limiting is not configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the API gateway management API to retrieve throttling settings for the relevant API stage or route configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A numeric value greater than 0 (e.g., 100.0 requests/second) confirms rate limiting is enabled. Null or absent value indicates no rate limiting at the stage level.

option_description: Whether the PII data channel enforces authentication before permitting data access. Authentication may be enforced at the API gateway, application layer, or network policy level. Unauthenticated channels allow any network-accessible client to initiate requests against PII data without identity verification.
security_impact: Referenced by the missing_rate_limiting_on_pii_channel Rego rule. The policy triggers an exposure when both rate_limiting_enabled is false and channel_authentication_required is false. Unauthenticated channels with no rate limiting create the highest exfiltration and enumeration risk because there is no identity binding to constrain or audit access, enabling anonymous automated harvesting of PII at full network throughput (MITRE T1020 Automated Exfiltration).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to access the PII endpoint without providing any authentication credentials or tokens. A 200 response confirms no authentication is required; 401 or 403 confirms authentication is enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'HTTP Status: 401' or 'HTTP Status: 403' confirms authentication is required. 'HTTP Status: 200' confirms the channel is unauthenticated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect API gateway route configurations, application middleware stacks, or network policy files to determine if authentication is enforced for the relevant endpoint or route group.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of authentication middleware or plugin enabled on the route confirms authentication is required. Absence or 'enabled: false' indicates the channel is unauthenticated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the API gateway console to verify whether an authorizer, API key requirement, or OAuth scope is attached to the resource method handling PII requests.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > API Gateway > [Select API] > Resources > [Select Resource] > [Select Method] > Method Request > Authorization (must not be NONE) and API Key Required: true
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Authorization showing a Lambda authorizer, Cognito User Pool, or IAM, combined with API Key Required: true, confirms authentication is enforced. 'NONE' authorization indicates the channel is unauthenticated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review documented security requirements or architecture decision records with the development and platform teams to confirm whether authentication was intentionally omitted (e.g., for public data endpoints) or represents a gap.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written documentation confirming authentication enforcement, or confirmation from the team that the endpoint is intentionally public. Ambiguity or lack of documentation suggests authentication may not be consistently enforced.

option_description: Controls whether the HTTP/S channel exposes endpoints that permit bulk or paginated retrieval of PII records without per-request quantity limits, such as list-all, export, or unbounded search endpoints. A value of true means such endpoints exist and are reachable without effective throttling on result set size.
security_impact: Referenced by the missing_rate_limiting_on_pii_channel Rego rule: when bulk_export_endpoint_exposed is true and rate_limiting_enabled is false, the exposure fires unconditionally regardless of authentication state. This means an authenticated but malicious insider or a compromised credential holder can harvest the entire PII dataset in a single automated session, directly enabling T1020 (Automated Exfiltration) and T1030 (Data Transfer Size Limits) attack patterns.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the OpenAPI/Swagger specification for the service and search for endpoints with operation IDs or paths suggesting bulk retrieval (e.g., /export, /bulk, /list, /search without a mandatory 'limit' parameter marked as required).
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s https://<host>/openapi.json | jq '[.paths | to_entries[] | select(.key | test("/export|/bulk|/list|/all"; "i")) | {path: .key, methods: (.value | keys)}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array listing matching endpoint paths; empty array indicates no obvious bulk endpoints. Verify each hit manually for required limit parameters.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect API gateway or reverse proxy configuration (e.g., Kong, NGINX, AWS API Gateway) for route definitions that lack max_body_size or pagination enforcement middleware on PII-serving routes.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Route entries without an associated rate-limit plugin or page-size validation rule indicate bulk endpoint exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send a test request to a suspected list/export endpoint without a page size or limit parameter and measure the response payload size. If the response returns more than a configured threshold of records, the endpoint is unbounded.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{size_download}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://<host>/api/v1/users' | awk '{if($1>102400) print "UNBOUNDED: " $1 " bytes"; else print "BOUNDED: " $1 " bytes"}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response sizes consistently above 100 KB for a single unaided request indicate an unbounded bulk endpoint.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the API development team or review data dictionary / API contract documents to enumerate all endpoints that return collections of user records and confirm whether mandatory server-side pagination limits are enforced at the application layer rather than only as optional client hints.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation explicitly stating a maximum page size (e.g., max 100 records per request) enforced server-side; absence of such documentation is a finding.

typical_values: true (common in legacy internal APIs and data export services)
false (modern APIs with enforced pagination limits)

option_description: Controls whether BGP peers apply RPKI Route Origin Validation (ROV) to filter BGP announcements, ensuring that only autonomous systems listed in a valid Route Origin Authorization (ROA) can originate a given IP prefix. Prevents unauthorized ASes from attracting traffic by announcing prefixes they do not own.
security_impact: Referenced by the bgp_route_hijacking_exposure Rego rule: when both rpki_route_origin_validation_enabled and traffic_path_uses_private_interconnect are false, the BGP hijacking exposure fires regardless of transport encryption state. A second rule fires when these two flags are false even if encryption is present, recognizing that RPKI protects the routing layer independently of payload encryption. Without ROV, adversaries can perform prefix hijacking (T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle, T1599 Network Boundary Bridging) to redirect PII traffic through attacker-controlled ASes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a self-operated BGP router running BIRD, inspect the RPKI validator configuration and confirm ROV is applied to all peering sessions.
how_to_obtain.command: birdc 'show protocols all' | grep -A5 'rpki\|ROV\|route_origin' && birdc 'show route filtered' | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RPKI protocol in 'Established' state; import filter referencing an ROV check function applied to external BGP sessions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Validate that ROA records exist for your announced prefixes using the Routinator CLI or the RIPE NCC RPKI validator, confirming your prefixes are covered by valid ROAs.
how_to_obtain.command: routinator vrps --format csv | grep '<your-AS-number>' && curl -s 'https://stat.ripe.net/data/rpki-validation/data.json?resource=<your-prefix>&sourceapp=sec-assessment' | jq '.data.validating_roas'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CSV output listing your prefix/ASN pairs with 'Valid' status; JSON response showing matching ROA entries with maxLength coverage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use Cloudflare's RPKI validator web interface or the Routinator web UI to check whether your upstream transit provider enforces ROV by testing a known invalid route.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Navigate to https://rpki.cloudflare.com/ → 'Check an ASN or Prefix' → enter your announced prefix → verify 'Valid' status. Then contact ISP/transit provider NOC to confirm they drop RPKI-invalid routes on peering sessions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Prefix shows 'Valid' status with matching ROA. ISP confirms 'RPKI invalid routes are rejected' in writing or via policy documentation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Contact your upstream ISP or colocation BGP peer and request written confirmation of their ROV enforcement policy on peering sessions, referencing their published MANRS (Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security) participation status.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: MANRS API returns filtering action compliance as true; ISP NOC confirms ROV is enforced on all customer-facing BGP sessions.

typical_values: false (default; majority of networks do not enforce ROV as of 2024)
true (large CDNs, tier-1 ISPs, MANRS participants)

option_description: Controls whether PII-bearing HTTP/S traffic between the client and application endpoint traverses a private network interconnect (dedicated leased line, AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, Google Cloud Interconnect, or SD-WAN with a private backbone) rather than the public internet BGP routing fabric, eliminating exposure to public AS path manipulation.
security_impact: Referenced by the bgp_route_hijacking_exposure Rego rule as the primary mitigation: when traffic_path_uses_private_interconnect is true, the BGP hijacking exposure does not fire regardless of RPKI or encryption state. Private interconnects bypass public BGP routing entirely, removing the attack surface for T1557 and T1599. When false, the rule requires both RPKI validation and transport encryption to suppress the exposure, making private interconnect the strongest single control against BGP-layer attacks on PII flows.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run traceroute from the client network to the application endpoint IP and inspect each hop's ASN. Any hops in public ASNs between client and server confirm public internet traversal.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All hops between client and application should show internal RFC1918 addresses or private peering ASNs (e.g., your own AS or a known private peering partner). Any public ASN hops indicate public internet traversal.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the AWS Console, verify that a Direct Connect connection exists between the client's on-premises network and the VPC hosting the application, and confirm traffic is routed via the Virtual Private Gateway rather than an internet gateway.
how_to_obtain.command: aws directconnect describe-connections --query 'connections[*].{Name:connectionName,State:connectionState,Bandwidth:bandwidth,Location:location}' --output table && aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters 'Name=tag:Environment,Values=production' --query 'RouteTables[*].Routes[?GatewayId!=null]' --output json
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → Direct Connect → Connections (verify 'available' state) → Virtual Interfaces → confirm private VIF attached to target VPC's Virtual Private Gateway.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Direct Connect connection in 'available' state with a private VIF; VPC route tables showing traffic to client CIDR via vgw-* (Virtual Private Gateway) rather than igw-* (Internet Gateway).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SD-WAN or MPLS configuration files to confirm that routes for the application endpoint's subnet are pinned to the private WAN fabric and not redistributed to or from internet-facing interfaces.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy entries routing application subnet traffic exclusively via private transport (MPLS or private broadband) with no 'direct internet access' fallback for PII endpoints.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review network architecture diagrams with the network engineering team and confirm a formal change control record exists for the private interconnect provisioning, including circuit IDs and SLA documentation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Architecture diagram explicitly labels the path as 'private interconnect' with circuit ID; change record confirms no public internet fallback is configured for PII application traffic.

typical_values: false (default; most client-to-application flows use public internet)
true (enterprise B2B integrations, financial sector, healthcare networks with dedicated circuits)

option_description: Controls whether strong transport-layer encryption (TLS 1.2 or higher) is mandatorily applied end-to-end for all PII-bearing HTTP/S traffic, with plaintext fallback disabled, HTTPS-only enforcement active, and certificate validation preventing fraudulent certificate acceptance on redirected paths.
security_impact: Referenced by the bgp_route_hijacking_exposure Rego rule as a compensating control: even when traffic traverses public internet without RPKI, enforced transport encryption means hijacked traffic remains confidential. However, the rule still fires when both private interconnect and RPKI are absent even with encryption, acknowledging that encryption alone does not prevent traffic redirection. Additionally, transport_encryption_enforced is evaluated independently in plaintext_transmission and tls_downgrade_attack rules, where its absence triggers high-criticality score-8 exposures covering T1048.003 and T1040.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use testssl.sh or nmap ssl-enum-ciphers to verify that the application endpoint only accepts TLS 1.2+ connections and that HTTP plaintext connections are rejected or redirected with HSTS.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: testssl.sh shows TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 as 'offered', SSLv2/SSLv3/TLS 1.0/TLS 1.1 as 'not offered'; HTTP plaintext returns 301/302 to HTTPS URL with Strict-Transport-Security header present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the web server or load balancer TLS configuration for minimum protocol version settings and verify plaintext HTTP listeners are disabled or redirect-only.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ssl_protocols directive showing only 'TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3'; no plaintext listener on port 80 without an unconditional redirect to HTTPS.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS Certificate Manager or the cloud provider's load balancer API to confirm the SSL policy applied to all HTTPS listeners enforces a minimum of TLS 1.2.
how_to_obtain.command: aws elbv2 describe-listeners --load-balancer-arn <alb-arn> --query 'Listeners[*].{Port:Port,Protocol:Protocol,SslPolicy:SslPolicy}' --output table && aws elbv2 describe-ssl-policies --names ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 --query 'SslPolicies[*].{Name:Name,Protocols:SslProtocols}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All port-443 listeners show an SSL policy of 'ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06' or equivalent; no listener on port 80 without redirect action.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify certificate pinning or strict CA bundle validation is configured on the client side by inspecting application configuration or compiled trust store settings, ensuring hijacked paths cannot present fraudulent certificates.
how_to_obtain.command: openssl s_client -connect <application-endpoint>:443 -verify 5 -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'Verify return code|Certificate chain|subject|issuer'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows 'Verify return code: 0 (ok)' with certificate chain terminating at a recognized public CA; any self-signed or unknown CA is a finding.

typical_values: false (default schema value; plaintext APIs still common in internal microservice meshes)
true (externally-facing production APIs, PCI-DSS and HIPAA-scoped endpoints)

option_description: Controls whether the DNS resolver used by the client (stub resolver, OS resolver, or recursive resolver) enforces DNSSEC signature validation for the application endpoint's domain, ensuring that DNS responses are cryptographically authenticated and that unsigned or tampered responses are rejected rather than acted upon.
security_impact: Referenced by the dns_spoofing_redirect_of_flow Rego rule: when both dnssec_validation_enabled and dns_over_encrypted_transport are false, the DNS spoofing exposure fires unconditionally, including even when certificate_pinning_enabled is also false. A second rule fires when the first two are false regardless of pinning state. DNS spoofing without DNSSEC allows attackers to redirect the PII data flow to an adversary-controlled server before TLS is established, enabling T1584.002 (DNS Server compromise) and T1590.002 (DNS reconnaissance and targeting) attack chains.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the application endpoint domain with DNSSEC validation enabled on a known-validating resolver and confirm the AD (Authenticated Data) bit is set in the response, indicating successful DNSSEC validation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response flags line includes 'ad' bit (e.g., 'flags: qr rd ra ad'); RRSIG record present in ANSWER section; DS record visible in parent zone confirming delegation signer chain.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the recursive resolver configuration (BIND, Unbound, systemd-resolved) on the client system for DNSSEC validation directives.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Unbound: 'auto-trust-anchor-file' directive present with root anchor; BIND: 'dnssec-validation yes' or 'dnssec-validation auto'; systemd-resolved: 'DNSSEC=yes' or 'DNSSEC=allow-downgrade' (note: allow-downgrade is a partial finding).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test whether the client's configured resolver rejects DNSSEC-invalid responses by querying a known DNSSEC-broken domain and confirming SERVFAIL is returned.
how_to_obtain.command: dig @$(grep nameserver /etc/resolv.conf | head -1 | awk '{print $2}') dnssec-failed.org A +time=5 | grep -E 'status:|SERVFAIL|NOERROR'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response status shows 'SERVFAIL' confirming the resolver is performing and enforcing DNSSEC validation. 'NOERROR' with an IP address indicates validation is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the DNSSEC Analyzer web tool to verify the application endpoint domain has a complete and valid DNSSEC chain of trust from root to the authoritative zone.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Navigate to https://dnssec-analyzer.verisignlabs.com/ → enter the application domain → review chain of trust visualization for green checkmarks on all delegation points (root → TLD → domain → record).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All delegation points show green status; DS records present at each delegation boundary; no broken chain or missing signatures.

typical_values: false (default; most enterprise resolvers do not enforce DNSSEC validation)
true (government networks, some financial sector deployments, ISPs with DNSSEC-validating recursive resolvers)

option_description: Controls whether DNS queries for the application endpoint are transmitted over an encrypted channel using DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH, RFC 8484) or DNS-over-TLS (DoT, RFC 7858), preventing network-path observers from reading or modifying DNS query/response content in transit between the client and its configured upstream resolver.
security_impact: Referenced by the dns_spoofing_redirect_of_flow Rego rule alongside dnssec_validation_enabled: when both are false, the DNS spoofing exposure fires unconditionally. DoH/DoT encrypts the DNS transport channel, preventing on-path adversaries from intercepting DNS queries to perform cache poisoning or spoofed response injection (T1584.002). While DoH/DoT does not replace DNSSEC's origin authentication, it closes the passive interception vector by which attackers identify and time their spoofing attempts.
