how_to_obtain.instruction: Check systemd-resolved configuration for DNS-over-TLS enforcement, or inspect browser enterprise policy for DoH resolver configuration.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'DNSOverTLS|DNS=|FallbackDNS' /etc/systemd/resolved.conf 2>/dev/null && resolvectl status | grep -E 'DNS over TLS|DNS Servers|Current DNS' && cat /etc/firefox/policies/policies.json 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool | grep -A5 'DNSOverHTTPS'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: systemd-resolved shows 'DNSOverTLS=yes' (not 'opportunistic'); resolvectl status confirms 'DNS over TLS: yes'; Firefox policy shows 'Enabled: true' with a specific DoH provider URL.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture DNS traffic on the client's primary network interface and confirm that no plaintext UDP/TCP port-53 DNS queries are sent for the application endpoint's domain.
how_to_obtain.command: sudo tcpdump -i any -c 50 -n 'port 53' 2>/dev/null & sleep 5; dig <application-domain> A; wait; echo '--- check above for port 53 traffic ---'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No port-53 DNS packets captured during the dig command; if DoH/DoT is enforced, DNS traffic will appear only on port 853 (DoT) or port 443 (DoH) and will be encrypted/unreadable to tcpdump.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify DoT connectivity directly to the configured encrypted resolver by establishing a TLS connection on port 853 and sending a test query.
how_to_obtain.command: kdig -d @1.1.1.1 +tls-ca +tls-host=cloudflare-dns.com <application-domain> A 2>&1 | grep -E 'TLS handshake|Received|status:' || echo 'kdig not available; try: openssl s_client -connect 1.1.1.1:853 -servername cloudflare-dns.com </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E Verify'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: kdig shows 'TLS handshake OK' and a valid DNS response with status NOERROR; openssl confirms 'Verify return code: 0 (ok)' on port 853.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Google Chrome or Edge, navigate to the secure DNS settings page and verify that 'Use secure DNS' is enabled with a specific DoH provider (not 'With your current service provider' which may be unencrypted).
how_to_obtain.navigation: Chrome: Settings → Privacy and security → Security → 'Use secure DNS' → verify toggle is ON and a specific provider (e.g., Cloudflare, Google, custom) is selected. Edge: Settings → Privacy, search, and services → Security → 'Use secure DNS'.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure DNS toggle is enabled; a named DoH provider or custom DoH URL is configured; 'With your current service provider' is not selected (this option does not guarantee encryption).

typical_values: false (default; OS-level DoH/DoT disabled in most enterprise environments due to split-DNS concerns)
true (consumer browsers with secure DNS enabled, Zero Trust network clients, mobile MDM-enforced DoH profiles)

option_description: Controls whether the client application enforces certificate pinning (also called SSL/TLS pinning) for the application endpoint, binding the expected server certificate or public key hash into the client application itself so that TLS handshakes with certificates not matching the pin are rejected — even if the certificate is issued by a trusted CA or if DNS was spoofed to redirect the connection.
security_impact: Referenced by the dns_spoofing_redirect_of_flow Rego rule as a compensating control: when certificate_pinning_enabled is true, the DNS spoofing exposure requires both dnssec_validation_enabled and dns_over_encrypted_transport to also be false before it fires (the second rule fires regardless of pinning, but the first rule requires all three to be absent). Pinning ensures that even a successful DNS spoofing attack (T1584.002) redirecting to an adversary-controlled server cannot complete a fraudulent TLS handshake, as the rogue certificate will not match the pinned hash, directly blocking T1557 adversary-in-the-middle scenarios.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect mobile application manifests or native client source code for pinned certificate hashes using TrustKit, OkHttp CertificatePinner, or equivalent libraries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: network_security_config.xml contains <pin-set> elements with <pin digest='SHA-256'> entries for the application domain; source code shows CertificatePinner.Builder with .add() calls containing sha256/ hashes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check web application or API client configuration for HPKP (Public-Key-Pins) header emission or application-framework-level pinning libraries (e.g., Requests with custom transport adapters in Python, axios with custom httpsAgent in Node.js).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: References to Public-Key-Pins header construction or pinning library imports with specific hash values; importantly, 'rejectUnauthorized: false' or 'cert_reqs=CERT_NONE' indicates pinning is actively disabled, which is a critical finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Using a transparent HTTPS intercepting proxy (mitmproxy) on the same network, attempt to intercept the client's connection to the application endpoint with a dynamically-generated certificate and observe whether the client aborts the connection.
how_to_obtain.command: mitmproxy --mode transparent --ssl-insecure -p 8080 &  # route client traffic through proxy; observe in mitmproxy console whether the client accepts or rejects the intercepted certificate
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Client aborts the TLS handshake or displays a certificate error rather than completing the connection; mitmproxy log shows 'Connection killed' or 'SSL handshake failed' from the client side, confirming pinning is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the application's security documentation, threat model, or mobile security assessment reports for explicit mention of certificate pinning implementation, including pin rotation procedures and emergency bypass processes.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Security documentation explicitly states that certificate pinning is implemented with specific pin hashes, backup pins, and a documented pin rotation procedure; absence of rotation documentation with pinning enabled is a secondary finding.

typical_values: false (default; most web applications and many mobile apps do not implement pinning due to operational complexity of pin rotation)
true (banking and financial mobile apps, government mobile clients, high-security API SDKs)
